records.name: Malacca
records.summary:
Malacca enforces the national framework with no documented local mitigation: same-sex conduct is criminalised (up to 20 years and whipping), there is no legal gender recognition, and public-morality policing runs through the state's religious authority — the agency type international monitoring identifies as the driver of state-backed discrimination against LGBT people in Malaysia.

The heritage-tourism setting offers no recorded protection; visible gender nonconformity is exposed to that religious enforcement.

records.name: Abuja Federal Capital Territory
records.summary: Worse than national: the killing of the territory's most publicly visible trans person, followed by a refusal to investigate. On 8 August 2024 a 33-year-old transgender woman with a large TikTok following ('Abuja Area Mama') was found beaten and bruised beside the Katampe-Mabushi Expressway hours after posting a routine video, having previously expressed fear for her life; a human-rights group has since sued the federal government and the police for failing to investigate, seeking a court order compelling investigation and prosecution after multiple petitions were ignored — which qualifies the killing under the state-failure test rather than leaving it a lone incident. Reporting on the capital's queer scene documents threats and raids alongside informal community organising. The national framework applies here unchanged: same-sex conduct criminalised with up to 14 years' imprisonment, with dating-app 'kito' gangs a nationwide pattern; the UK's foreign office warned LGBT travellers in August 2026 of arrest, violence, attacks and blackmail risks. Scored relative to the national score (0.08) for Nigeria.

freshness.fact: Current (19 Aug 2026): UK advisory cites attacks, 14-year SSMPA terms and sharia death-penalty risk; FCT remains federal enforcement hub.
The Aug 2024 Abuja death of a trans creator remains a live enforcement/climate marker; nothing superseding found.

records.name: Lima
records.summary:
Lima concentrates the country's sharpest documented lethality and its newest legal restriction. An LGBTI human-rights observatory at a national university counted 54 LGBTI+ murders for 2020–2023, with trans women the most affected, amid rising hate crimes. In 2025 the national congress — sitting and operating out of the capital — approved a norm against trans people's use of public bathrooms (committee vote February 2025; floor vote April 2025), which a national human-rights institute published an analysis calling legalised discrimination with direct consequences for access to public space.

For a trans visitor, the capital is therefore where both mechanisms bite: the bathroom-restriction norm is national policy administered here, and the murder pattern shows the violence risk when prosecutions are rare and official statistics thin.

records.name: Municipalidad Metropolitana de Lima
records.summary: Model estimate (route 3, best-knowledge delta): capital metro — the entire scene (NGOs including MHOL), anonymity of 10 million; Miraflores/Barranco visitor districts experience a normal Latin-urban climate. Its own sources sharpen the picture: the Congressional Women and Family Committee unanimously approved bills barring trans people from public toilets of the sex assigned at birth (20 Feb 2025; the plenary approved the fused text on 2 April 2025, with custody, medical, caregiving and disability exceptions), and the international airport relabeled its bathrooms to "women in their diversity / men in their diversity" after a 2023 complaint. A university observatory counted 54 LGBTQ+ killings and 170 rights violations 2020-2023, 30 of the dead trans women; in Feb 2023 a 31-year-old trans sex worker was abducted from central Lima's Chancay street by a criminal gang and shot dead. Scored relative to the national score (0.36) for Peru.

records.name: Ankara
records.summary:
Ankara is the administrative core of what the country's leading LGBTI rights organisation — reporting from its capital launch event in 2025 — documented as hostility turned into explicit state policy: presidency-centred targeting, the family ministry as implementing body, broadcast and platform censorship, an LGBTI organisation closed, six violations of the right to life (three recorded as hate-motivated) with trans people most affected, and no official hate-crime statistics in existence. A leaked October 2025 judicial package would add up to three years' imprisonment for conduct contrary to biological sex and its promotion, and bar gender-affirming care below age 25.

The capital hosts the machinery that drafts and enforces those measures; nothing on record shows local countervailing protection, and the same courts and ministries that field the report operate here.

records.name: Eskişehir
records.summary: Model estimate (route 3, best-knowledge delta): Eskişehir — university city, the most youthful-anonymous interior city; Amnesty's 2024 provincial monitoring records that authorities unlawfully prevented its Pride march, in a city that had previously hosted one of the country's few functioning pride events. National frame: the leaked October 2025 draft would criminalise 'conduct contrary to biological sex' and its promotion (up to 3 years) and restrict gender-affirming care (minimum age 25); a 2025 rights report records hostility as explicit state policy, six violations of the right to life, trans people most affected. Scored relative to the national score (0.15) for Turkey.

records.name: Gaziantep
records.summary:
Gaziantep sits fully under the national framework with no documented local divergence in either direction: the leaked October 2025 judicial package would criminalise conduct contrary to biological sex and its promotion (up to three years) and restrict gender-affirming care to age 25 and above, while the 2025 national rights report documents hostility as explicit state policy — presidency-centred targeting, censorship, an organisation closed, six violations of the right to life with trans people most affected, and no official protection statistics at all.

Nothing in the record shows this province offering either special danger beyond, or protection beneath, that national baseline; a visibly trans visitor's exposure is the national one, locally enforced.

records.name: İstanbul
records.summary: Model estimate (route 3, best-knowledge delta): İstanbul — the whole scene; the Beyoğlu legacy: the district governor's office ordered trans women's apartments on Bayram Street sealed in March 2024; on 18 July 2025 a residential street was blockaded by police with drones and raids (three detained); on 31 July 2025 around 20 trans women were rounded up for identity checks while street, shopping and in cafés, taken to a police station, names recorded and videos filmed ('this is profiling'). Pride has been banned for a ninth consecutive year — 113 detained on 25 June 2023, 46 detained at the 2024 Acıbadem march with judicial controls and travel bans. Scored relative to the national score (0.15) for Turkey.
